quote.author: GoodPartsOnly
quote.name: Good Parts Only
quote.text:
A SpaceX competitor explains just how impossible it is to achieve what Elon has.

Rocket Lab CEO Peter Beck once said reusable rockets didn't make sense for small rockets like his Electron. He promised he'd eat his hat if he ever changed his mind.

In 2019, with SpaceX already landing rockets, he walked on stage and admitted he was wrong.

Then he explained why he'd doubted it. The rocket comes back at "eight and a half times the speed of sound," through plasma "about half the temperature of the sun," with loads like "three elephants" standing on "a 1.8 mm carbon fibre rocket."

"Getting through the wall is really, really hard."

SpaceX first landed an orbital-class rocket booster upright on December 21, 2015.

The first two features Matt Palmer walks through in his What's new in Grok Bot 1.0 video this morning, Team Bot improvements and bots that join your meetings, are the same two things I asked for right here on X. On August 30 I wrote that we need to be able to share Grok Bots across teams, and Elon replied "Coming soon." On October 25 I suggested the Grok Bot team let my bot join a Zoom or Teams call with me, or for me, and Elon replied "This might be possible." Meetings started switching on for users less than two weeks later, and now both features lead the 1.0 release.

That says a lot about how responsive this team is. A user describes a need, Elon weighs in himself, and within weeks it is in the product and getting better. Any bot can now become a Team Bot at the flip of a switch, you choose exactly who it is shared with, and a new analytics tab shows the hours it has saved. In a meeting, the bot listens, answers in the chat and picks up spoken instructions, pulling what you need from your connected tools while the meeting is still going. The tempo of Grok Bot's evolution is extraordinary. And these are only two of the many new features in 1.0, so watch Matt's video to see just how fast Grok Bot is improving. I'm grateful to Matt, the team and Elon for listening.

quote.author: ZhouTalks
quote.name: 周周聊搞钱
quote.text:
最近硅谷两大佬因为马斯克吵翻了，结果老马亲自下场，一句话把全网看乐了。

先是著名反垄断评论家 Matt 泼冷水：SpaceX 算什么奇迹？马斯克根本不是天才，无非是会找华尔街搞钱，用钞票和工程师硬堆出来的。

这话连平时谁都不服的硅谷传奇程序员 DHH 都看不下去了，直接回怼：太酸了！哪怕你不喜欢马斯克，也得承认他“把吹过的牛变成现实”的能力举世无双。从特斯拉、脑机接口到 SpaceX，世上有一百万个会搞钱的投资人，但只有一个马斯克。

随后马斯克本尊下场，只回了一句灵魂反问：“行，那你给我解释一下蓝色起源、波音和 ULA？”

这一刀，直接捅在了“唯金钱论”的肺管子上。

如果光靠砸钱就能上天，那现在的太空霸主绝不可能是 SpaceX：
1、 比谁更有钱？ 贝索斯的蓝色起源比 SpaceX 早成立两年，背后站着前世界首富，从来不缺钱，结果到现在还在努力追赶。

2、 比谁补贴多？ NASA 当年搞载人航天，同一个任务，给波音砸了 42 亿美元，给 SpaceX 只给了 26 亿。结果 SpaceX 从 2020 年就开始像公交车一样送宇航员上天，波音的飞船却连宇航员都接不回来，最后还得靠 SpaceX 去救场。

3、 比华尔街输血？ SpaceX 起步根本没有华尔街一分钱，全是马斯克卖掉 PayPal 后自己掏的 1 亿美元家底。猎鹰 1 号连炸三次后差点破产，第四次才绝处逢生。

DHH 说得太对了：钱能买来顶级工程师，但买不来“不怕炸火箭”的魄力。

看看星舰第 15 次试飞（Flight 15）就懂了：同一个任务里，助推器在海里丢了，但飞船却从轨道返航、被发射塔的“机械筷子”稳稳夹住。

放在传统航天巨头那里，“丢了助推器”这半句话，就够他们停飞开两年的事故批斗会了；但在 SpaceX，这只是通往成功的又一组实验数据。

@elonmusk 说实话，到底哪个更难造：是一枚能上天的火箭，还是一家“允许工程师靠炸火箭来试错”的公司？

BREAKING: Texas A&M’s $205.5 million semiconductor project will help train America’s next generation of chipmakers for Terafab. 🇺🇸

University leaders say Terafab’s planned chip plant in Grimes County makes A&M’s Semiconductor Institute even more relevant, with Terafab counting on the institute to help attract talent. 

• $205.5 million project: The institute’s new building in Bryan and supporting water infrastructure will serve chip research, development and workforce training. 

• Practical training for Terafab jobs: Director Steve Putna says students will train in an environment designed to help them move smoothly into Terafab’s workforce.

• Access to engineering talent: Texas A&M graduates more than 5,000 engineers annually, giving nearby chipmakers a major source of potential recruits.

• Industry-style facilities: The institute will feature a cleanroom and six laboratories, giving students practical experience with semiconductor technology.

• Construction is progressing: The building is about 20% complete. Substantial completion is expected by the end of 2027, with significant operations planned for mid-2028. 

• Infrastructure for long-term growth: Regents just approved $14.2 million for a new well and storage system supporting the RELLIS campus, including the institute.

As a teenager, Elon Musk went through an existential crisis, reading religion and philosophy in search of the meaning of life

Then he discovered Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

“I ended up reading The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, which is actually a book on philosophy, just sort of disguised as a silly humor book. But it's actually a philosophy book. And Adams makes the point that it's actually the question that is harder than the answer”

A seemingly silly humor book helped a teenager searching for meaning realize something profound

Finding the right question is often harder than finding the answer

And that curiosity never left him

Today, it's driving him to build rockets, explore the universe, and push humanity toward the stars

Starlink helped rescue teams bring 211 stranded tourists to safety in Argentina’s remote mountains. ❤️🇦🇷

A snowstorm trapped dozens of vehicles near Balcón del Pissis, Catamarca. Snow blocked the roads, leaving tourists stranded in freezing conditions.

Satellite phones and @Starlink helped raise the alarm. Telecentro also supplied Starlink connectivity to strengthen communications between teams working in the mountains, where conventional networks were limited.

Firefighters, police, medical teams and local rescuers joined the operation as heavy machinery cleared paths through the snow.

Authorities confirmed 211 people were rescued, with 39 sheltered at a mining camp until they could descend safely.

A life-saving effort on the ground, supported by connectivity from space.

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
A lot of people have real trouble thinking about the aggregate behavior of groups. They can only think about individuals. 

So they think about Elon Musk as an individual. Maybe they think that he must be retarded, because they need that for emotional reasons. Or maybe they think he is a talented rocket designer. 

But even if they realize he understands rockets, they can only think about him as an individual doing tasks. Not about his impact on what the whole company does. 

If Elon Musk is just a talented rocket designer, then he can spend all day, every day, improving rocket designs. 

But he is just one of 7000 engineers. So even if did a perfect job, he would only improve progress by about .014% 

So, when a midwit looks at SpaceX, he sees 7000 engineers, and says to himself "Elon Musk cannot possibly be designing the whole damn rocket himself. These people are giving him too much credit."

This would be absolutely true if Musk were just a some random SpaceX engineer. But he isn't. He's the absolute dictator of the whole damn company. 

He decides, with absolute and unquestionable authority, which behaviors are punished and which are rewarded. 

Why is this important? 

When I worked at Boeing, on various classified projects, I naively came in with the assumption that I was a software engineer, employed to design and build functional software as quickly and cheaply as possible. 

Because of this, I focused on functionality and efficiency, for example suggesting changes that would obviate the need for entire projects and software components. 

And I very rapidly became persona non grata. 

At first, this caused me to adopt an air of aggrieved innocence. I was just trying to do my job well, and I was being punished for it. 

Then I gradually came to realize that I hadn't properly understood what my job was, or what the actual mission of Boeing Defense, Space, and Security was. 

Boeing DSS was not an aerospace company. Boeing DSS was a fraud company. 

Its goal was twofold. First, to maximize transfer of public tax dollars to stockholder pockets. Second, to maintain the appearance of being an aerospace company, to prevent the fraud from being exposed. 

Which meant that my real job was twofold. First, to generate billable hours. Second, to look busy. 

This is why Space Launch System sucks. Why it is always late when it doesn't fail outright. Why it is at 300% of its target budget. Why it leaves American astronauts stranded and needing a lift from SpaceX. 

That's because, for Boeing, building rockets is a side quest. Something they have to do to look busy. Yes, a rocket does occasionally fly, but that's just happening so programs don't get shut down. 

For Boeing, coming in early and under budget would actually be failure. The system is functioning exactly as designed. 

The cost, not the rocket, is the goal. 

Musk and SpaceX don't work like that. 

Unlike Boeing executives, Musk is not a useless grifter asshole. He is an entirely different kind of asshole... a rocket obsessed sperg. 

So, at SpaceX, engineers do not get rewarded for generating billable hours. They get rewarded for making rockets fly. And for all the subtasks of this, like figuring out how to make rockets lighter, figuring out how to make engines reignite better, figuring out how to make rocket exhaust not destroy launch pads, etc. 

And this attracts engineers who care about rockets. You've seen them on broadcasts, crying on open microphones because they dedicated their lives to something and it just flew. 

As a rocket engineer, who designs rockets, Musk is probably replaceable. As a rocket company engineer, who designs rocket companies, he is not. 

For over 50 years, the US space industry stagnated precisely for the lack of a Musk-like figure, who could not only create an effective aerospace company, but who could thereby demonstrate what an effective aerospace company looks like. 

Which makes it much more difficult for fraudsters to get away with fraud. 

I'm envious. I wish I could have worked for an aerospace company instead of a fraud company. 

But what's more important is that some of us now no longer have to play "who gets the most cheese?". 

They get to play "What can we build today?".

quote.name: Elon Musk
quote.text:
Let’s take this gentleman’s argument at face value that anyone can throw money at rockets and get something like Starship, Falcon or Dragon.

Perhaps he can explain to everyone how SpaceX is able to catch giant starships from orbit with chopsticks and deliver 85% of all Earth payload to orbit with Falcon, while Blue Origin, which started before SpaceX and was funded by the immensely wealthy Jeff Bezos, is not yet able to launch reliably?

Also, why is it that Boeing and Lockheed received several times what SpaceX did from the government for development of their rockets and spacecraft, but the Boeing capsule is still not operational and ULA delivers less than 5% of SpaceX payload to orbit?

I am genuinely curious about these questions.

Musk and SpaceX don't work like that. 

Unlike Boeing executives, Musk is not a useless grifter asshole. He is an entirely different kind of asshole... a rocket obsessed sperg. 

So, at SpaceX, engineers do not get rewarded for generating billable hours. They get rewarded for making rockets fly. And for all the subtasks of this, like figuring out how to make rockets lighter, figuring out how to make engines reignite better, figuring out how to make rocket exhaust not destroy launch pads, etc. 

And this attracts engineers who care about rockets. You've seen them on broadcasts, crying on open microphones because they dedicated their lives to something and it just flew. 

As a rocket engineer, who designs rockets, Musk is probably replaceable. As a rocket company engineer, who designs rocket companies, he is not. 

For over 50 years, the US space industry stagnated precisely for the lack of a Musk-like figure, who could not only create an effective aerospace company, but who could thereby demonstrate what an effective aerospace company looks like. 

Which makes it much more difficult for fraudsters to get away with fraud. 

I'm envious. I wish I could have worked for an aerospace company instead of a fraud company. 

But what's more important is that some of us now no longer have to play "who gets the most cheese?". 

They get to play "What can we build today?".

SpaceXSI’s Colossus I is helping fund $3.26 million in home repairs, paid local jobs and neighborhood improvements in South Memphis.

Memphis city government has approved the following investments using property tax revenue from the facility:

• $2 MILLION for home repairs through Memphis HOPE. Eligible properties can receive up to $25,000 for roof repairs, plumbing, heating, air conditioning and accessibility improvements.

• $309,282 for community grants supporting youth programs, public safety, workforce development and other services.

• $250,000 for paid jobs cleaning up and improving local neighborhoods.

• $250,000 to board up or demolish vacant properties.

• $150,000 to address neighborhood blight and deterioration.

• $125,000 for residents’ cooling and air-quality equipment, including air conditioners, fans, filters and air purifiers.

• $100,000 for environmental education.

• $50,000 for grants to organizations focused on health care.

• $25,000 for Memphis City Beautiful to support neighborhood cleanup and beautification.

All funding will benefit the designated five-mile area surrounding Colossus I.

Earlier community support from SpaceXSI and related initiatives includes:

• SCHOOL IMPROVEMENTS: Funded a completed gym renovation at Fairley High School and beautification work at John P. Freeman Optional School. Further school renovations are part of a broader $5 million investment program.

• YOUTH SUPPORT: A $350,000 donation through the Musk Foundation to the Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Memphis, highlighted in SpaceXSI’s community commitments. 

• ROAD CLEANUPS: SpaceXSI says its crews have cleared miles of local roads, removing more than 300 discarded mattresses, around 500 truck tires and over 15,000 pounds of debris.

• COMMUNITY CENTER SUPPORT: Partnered with Mt. Vernon Baptist Church to support fundraising for a new community center for local residents.

• POWER INFRASTRUCTURE: Invested $35 million in the first 150 MW substation serving Colossus, with construction funded by the company at no cost to Memphis Light, Gas and Water. 

• LOWER INTERNET BILLS: SpaceX introduced a 50% discount on Starlink Residential plans for Memphis and Southaven residents. The company says around 2,000 residents have already enrolled.

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
What was the significance of this weekend's SpaceX tower catch: 

"Catching the second stage is substantially harder than catching the first stage because the Ship returns from orbit while the booster returns from a short suborbital hop. The booster separates minutes after liftoff, performs a brief boostback, and comes back from only a few hundred kilometers away at relatively low speed. Ship must reach orbital velocity, deploy payload, coast for many hours, execute a precise deorbit burn, survive full reentry heating, and only then perform its landing burn. As such, Ship must carry a functional heat shield, fly a long guided atmospheric trajectory from the other side of the planet, and execute a high-energy flip into the “chopsticks” while protecting its heat-shield side. Those combined demands of orbital energy, thermal protection, long-range guidance, and final precision are why a Ship catch is so incredibly difficult. No prior system, including the Space Shuttle, recovered a rocket-style orbital stage in this manner. The catch validates the path to full reusability which is the foundation of Starship’s cost and cadence targets. This is particularly important in driving the economics of orbital data centers." - DB

posts.text: We've all read about Elon's working style being different. Hands-on, to say the least. Here's my anecdotal Elon moment: in 2014, we were raising capital and got introduced to John Doerr through our friend Jerry Murdock, and John wanted to meet me and Nami in Sicily, where they had a private event. During the evening, we jumped on a small bus together with Elon to join a dinner. At that time, Tesla had just opened their first showroom in Sweden, Täby. I told Elon that I booked a test ride with their new Model S but was wondering why they had a two-month waiting time to try the car. He was shocked/frustrated about the waiting time. He picked up his phone, made a call and sent some messages. The next week, Tesla Sweden called me and said, "Hi, you signed up for the test drive. We just got many more demo cars delivered and you can come and try it today already." That's how you get shit done! Can't even imagine how he operates today, but I'm sure it's still in the details and solving problems. That was inspiring, to say the least.

posts.text:
Morgan Stanley’s Adam Jonas on @SpaceX successfully catching Starship on flight 15:

“In our view, Flight 15 is a historic inflection moment for the company and spaceflight as a whole. SpaceX has recovered three Starship + many hundreds of Falcon 9 boosters in its history, and now others have accomplished the same. However, no entity has ever even attempted to recover a rocket upper stage in history (not counting Space Shuttle) given the intense thermal and mechanical stress of orbital re-entry. 

With an upper stage now recovered intact, SpaceX can conduct a deep inspection of Ship 42 and use the findings to improve future vehicles in a way that was never previously possible. We believe it also helps clear the path to ramping full reuse of both booster and ship, the last major technical milestone before weekly or even daily Starship flights become realistic.

With a ship catch, SpaceX has materially de-risked the longer-term TAMs across all 3 of its segments.”

We believe it also helps clear the path to ramping full reuse of both booster and ship, the last major technical milestone before weekly or even daily Starship flights become realistic.

With a ship catch, SpaceX has materially de-risked the longer-term TAMs across all 3 of its segments.”

quote.text:
Elon Musk reveals he recruited SpaceX’s first engineers by telling them 'we’re probably going to die', and ended up as chief engineer because no good one would join

“So SpaceX, I started that in mid-2002 expecting to fail. Probably 90% chance of failing.”

“And even when recruiting people, I didn’t try to make out that it would work. I said, we’re probably going to die, but there’s a small chance we might not die, and this is the only way to get people to Mars and advance the state of the art.”

“And then I ended up being chief engineer of the rocket, not because I wanted to, but because I couldn’t hire anyone who was good. None of the good chief engineers would join, because they’re like, this is too risky, you’re going to die. And so I ended up being chief engineer of the rocket.”

Samsung will invest $1.9 billion to expand its chip plant in Austin, Texas, to produce semiconductors for @SpaceX's Starlink satellites.

The factory is expected to produce STM32V8 chips used in Starlink's laser communication systems, shifting production currently based in France to the U.S.

The chips use an advanced 18nm FD-SOI process designed for high performance, low power consumption, and durability in harsh space environments.

Production is targeted to begin by 2030, according to the Seoul Economic Daily.

Let’s take this gentleman’s argument at face value that anyone can throw money at rockets and get something like Starship, Falcon or Dragon.

Perhaps he can explain to everyone how SpaceX is able to catch giant starships from orbit with chopsticks and deliver 85% of all Earth payload to orbit with Falcon, while Blue Origin, which started before SpaceX and was funded by the immensely wealthy Jeff Bezos, is not yet able to launch reliably?

Also, why is it that Boeing and Lockheed received several times what SpaceX did from the government for development of their rockets and spacecraft, but the Boeing capsule is still not operational and ULA delivers less than 5% of SpaceX payload to orbit?

I am genuinely curious about these questions.

BREAKING: Dominican Republic Government advances plans to expand Starlink connectivity and explores Grok for education. 🇩🇴

President Luis Abinader met with SpaceX executives and the Instituto Tecnológico de las Américas (ITLA) to discuss the initiatives:

• More than 50,000 Starlink antennas are already installed across the country.

• Starlink is already benefiting 1,608 students at ITLA’s Pedernales and Cotuí campuses.

• Further expansion would bring internet to communities and schools where traditional services are limited or unavailable.

• Grok Tutor is being considered for personalized learning support, helping students develop reasoning and critical thinking with teacher supervision.

• Its potential integration would support RD Inteligente, a Government program aiming to train one million Dominicans in AI.

• Location updates every second.
• A 24/7 control center receives automatic collision-risk alerts so operators can intervene.
